questions.question: Why does BFS find the path with the fewest edges in an unweighted graph?
options: It always explores the neighbour with the smallest label first
It uses recursion, which naturally finds short paths
It visits nodes in order of their distance (in edges) from the start, so the first time it reaches a node is via a shortest path
It tries every possible path and keeps the shortest
questions.explanation: BFS processes nodes ring by ring using a FIFO queue: all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on. The first arrival at any node is therefore along a fewest-edge path.

questions.question: In BFS, when should you mark a node as visited?
options: When it is added to the queue
When it is removed from the queue
After all its neighbours have been processed
Only when it is the goal node
questions.explanation: Marking on enqueue prevents the same node from being added to the queue multiple times by different neighbours.

questions.question: What are the time and space costs of an adjacency matrix for a graph with V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V + E) space; O(degree) to check an edge
O(V^2) space; O(1) to check whether an edge exists
O(E) space; O(E) to check an edge
O(V) space; O(log V) to check an edge
questions.explanation: A V x V matrix always uses O(V^2) space regardless of E, but answers 'is there an edge u-v?' in O(1). Adjacency lists use O(V + E) and suit sparse graphs.

questions.question: During DFS on an undirected graph, which observation indicates a cycle?
options: A node has more than two neighbours
A neighbour is already visited and is not the parent you arrived from
questions.explanation: In an undirected graph every edge appears in both directions, so the parent is always a visited neighbour. Any other visited neighbour means a second route back, which forms a cycle.
